abstract: Full conformal prediction usually relies on exchangeable data and symmetric fitting, excluding order-sensitive predictors and leaving coverage vulnerable to drift. Our extension separates two roles: fixed calibration weights in [0,1] emphasize observations expected to resemble the test point, while fixed algorithm tags encode information used by nonsymmetric fitting. A data-independent weighted random swap moves the candidate test point to a sampled position before fitting, with tags retained at their positions. This makes miscoverage imply membership in a high-residual set with weighted mass at most alpha. Comparing swapped and original residual-vector distributions yields finite-sample coverage at least 1 - alpha minus their weighted total-variation discrepancy. Under exchangeability this discrepancy vanishes even with nonsymmetric fitting; otherwise, a small discrepancy bounds undercoverage, not exact nominal validity. With distinct residuals, small discrepancy and normalized test weight also limit overcoverage; related bounds extend to split conformal and jackknife+. Simulations and electricity data distinguish calibration gains from width gains: on ordered electricity data, residual weighting improves coverage but widens intervals, whereas adding weighted fitting gives 89.3% coverage and narrower intervals than unweighted fitting, against a 90% target. Permutation removes the width advantage, and election-data coverage also remains below target.
methods: Weighted quantiles and nonsymmetric fitting prevent the usual exchangeable-rank argument. Prespecify calibration weights w_i in [0,1] and algorithm tags; normalize by D = 1 + sum_i w_i, assigning test weight 1/D. Draw K independently of the data using these normalized weights, swap the candidate test point with position K, and fit with tags fixed at their positions. At the true response, the test residual becomes entry K of the swapped-sequence residual vector. Replacing the test residual by infinity and using the test weight's dominance over calibration weights show that miscoverage implies entry K exceeds that vector's weighted (1 - alpha)-quantile. Such high-residual indices have total normalized weight at most alpha for every vector. Independence allows averaging their probabilities over K. Total variation bounds the change in each probability between swapped and original residual-vector distributions, yielding miscoverage at most alpha plus the weighted discrepancy, without fitting symmetry or stability.
results: Table 2 distinguishes improved calibration from narrower intervals on the ordered electricity-transfer data. Keeping least-squares fitting fixed, weighting calibration residuals raises coverage from 85.2% to 89.0% but increases mean width from 0.565 to 0.606. Retaining residual weighting and adding weighted least-squares fitting gives 89.3% coverage and reduces width to 0.527, below the unweighted baseline's 0.565. Thus calibration weighting improves coverage here at a width cost, while weighted fitting offsets that cost; neither weighted method reaches the 90% target. Uniformly permuting the same data creates an exchangeable control: coverage is 89.9%, 90.8%, and 90.8% for unweighted, residual-weighted, and additionally weighted-fit methods, respectively, with widths 0.639, 0.652, and 0.663. The observed width advantage disappears after permutation. These time-averaged comparisons do not guarantee 90% coverage under arbitrary drift: the theoretical lower bound is near nominal only when the weighted total-variation discrepancy between original and swapped residual-vector distributions is small.
notes: Coverage guarantees are marginal over data and the random swap. Theorem 2b supplies the swap-to-tail-mass argument; Table 2 separates calibration weighting from fitting and tests whether the width benefit survives permutation. Clarify the experimental swap implementation: descriptions cite equation (14), whereas the nonsymmetric guarantee uses randomized equation (20). Table 2 averages over time and supplies neither uncertainty estimates nor explicit width units; do not infer significance or units. For the upper bound, residuals must be distinct; small discrepancy and normalized test weight limit conservatism. The jackknife+ lower bound starts at 1 - 2 alpha.
